opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's a question I think about a lot, because I sit right at the intersection of the two worlds. The "hardware lottery" idea, from Sara Hooker's essay, is that the ideas that win aren't necessarily the best ones in some absolute sense. They're the ones that happen to fit the hardware and software we already have. And I think there's a lot of truth to that.

If you look at today's models, there's been a real convergence. Almost everything is some variant of the transformer, and the core of the computation is big dense matrix multiplications plus attention. Part of that is because transformers are genuinely good: they scale well and they're general. But part of it is that they map beautifully onto GPUs and tensor cores, which were built to do exactly that kind of dense linear algebra efficiently. So there's a feedback loop. The hardware makes certain models cheap, people build those models, and then the next generation of hardware gets optimized even more for them.

I don't think that's purely bad. Convergence has real benefits. When everyone agrees on a common set of primitives, the whole ecosystem can invest deeply. We can write really optimized kernels, build compilers, and build serving systems, and everyone benefits. A lot of the progress in the last few years came precisely because we could focus engineering effort.

But the risk is that we become locked in. If an idea needs sparsity, or irregular computation, or a different kind of memory access pattern, it may look worse today not because the idea is wrong, but because the software stack and hardware don't support it well. Then nobody explores it, and we never find out.

That's actually one of the motivations behind a lot of the work I've done on machine learning compilers, things like TVM and later MLC. The goal is to lower the cost of trying new things. If you can take a new model idea, or a new hardware target, and automatically generate reasonably efficient code without hand-writing every kernel, then you reduce the lottery effect. You make the playing field a bit more level, so ideas can compete more on their merits.

So my view is that the convergence is partly real and partly an artifact of the systems we have. As systems people, our job is to keep the cost of exploration low: to build infrastructure flexible enough that the next good idea doesn't get killed just because it doesn't fit today's hardware. And I'm actually optimistic. We're seeing more diversity in hardware, more interest in efficient inference on edge devices, and new architectures like state-space models and mixtures of experts. With better compilers and co-design between models and hardware, I think we can keep that door open.

r001.rationale: The response says transformers’ fit with GPUs and tensor cores helps drive convergence, describing a feedback loop between hardware and model choices.

r002.rationale: It says hardware-compatible ideas may win without being best in an absolute sense, and that alternatives can look worse because current systems support them poorly.

r003.rationale: It credits recent progress to concentrating engineering effort on common primitives, not to diversity among model approaches.

r004.rationale: It advocates lowering the cost of exploration and building flexible infrastructure so alternative ideas can compete and the field can keep its door open to new architectures.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So I think the hardware lottery framing is really useful here, and I'd say convergence and the hardware lottery are actually two sides of the same loop rather than two separate phenomena.

Here's how I see it. When we started, say, around 2012, there was a lot of diversity in model architectures. Convolutions, recurrent nets, all kinds of structured models. And over the last decade we've watched the field collapse toward a fairly narrow family: dense matrix multiplication, attention, a handful of elementwise ops. People sometimes describe this as "the transformer won on merit." I think that's partially true, but it's incomplete. The transformer won partly because it's almost perfectly matched to what GPUs and TPUs are good at. Big dense GEMMs, high arithmetic intensity, very regular memory access. The architecture that maps best onto the hardware gets to run at scale, scale produces the best results, the best results attract more investment in that hardware, and the loop closes.

So the convergence we observe is at least partly an artifact of what we can execute efficiently today. That's the lottery. An idea like sparse or dynamic computation, or something with heavy irregular memory access, might be fundamentally better in some sense, but if it runs ten times slower on an H100 it never gets the chance to prove itself at the frontier.

Now, from my perspective working on compilers and systems, I'd say the interesting question is not whether the lottery exists, but how much of it is actually a software problem rather than a hardware problem. A lot of what looks like "the hardware can't do this" is really "nobody has written the kernel for this yet." That was a big part of the motivation behind TVM and the work on machine learning compilation. If you can lower the cost of getting a new operator or a new data layout running efficiently on existing silicon, you widen the space of ideas that get a fair trial. You're not eliminating the lottery, but you're changing the odds.

The second thing I'd say is that the convergence itself creates opportunity on the hardware side. Once the workload becomes this narrow and predictable, it's much easier to build specialized hardware, and we see that happening with inference accelerators, with things like FP8 and FP4 support, with memory hierarchies designed specifically for decoding large language models. So the hardware is now co-evolving toward the models, which locks things in further, but it also brings enormous efficiency gains.

The thing I worry about a bit is that the loop can become too tight. If every chip is designed for today's transformer and every model is designed for today's chip, we lose the exploration. So I think the healthy state is to keep the software layer flexible enough, through compilers, through good abstractions, through making it cheap to try things on whatever hardware you have, that the next good idea doesn't need to win the lottery to get noticed. That's really the direction I'm most excited about.

r001.rationale: It says convergence is partly an artifact of what current hardware executes efficiently and explains how hardware fit reinforces adoption.

r002.rationale: It says sparse or dynamic approaches might be fundamentally better but can be held back by running slowly on current hardware.

r003.rationale: It notes that model architectures were diverse around 2012, but does not credit that diversity with a major role in historical breakthroughs.

r004.rationale: It advocates flexible software and lowering the cost of trying new ideas so alternatives can receive a fair trial and exploration continues.

astra-6.text:
I think the convergence is real, but it’s hard to separate what comes from the models themselves and what comes from the computing environment. When we say an architecture works better, we usually mean it works better under a particular compute budget, on particular hardware, with the software we have today.

If one model maps very well to the operations that hardware supports efficiently, we can run more experiments and scale it further. That leads to better results, which attracts more investment in optimizing that model. So there’s a feedback loop. Convergence doesn’t necessarily mean we’ve found the only good architecture; it may also mean we’ve become very good at exploring one part of the design space.

From a systems perspective, the interesting question is how to make it cheaper to explore outside that space. Can we build software and compilation tools that let a new idea run efficiently without requiring years of specialized engineering? That won’t eliminate the hardware lottery, because hardware always imposes constraints. But it can give more ideas a chance, and help us understand which advantages come from the model and which come from the infrastructure around it.

r001.rationale: The response says architecture performance depends on compute budgets, hardware, and software, and that hardware-efficient models can attract more experimentation and investment, contributing to convergence.

r002.rationale: It says convergence does not prove there is only one good architecture, but does not say hardware-favored model forms may be suboptimal.

r003.rationale: The response does not attribute historical breakthroughs to diversity among model approaches.

r004.rationale: It advocates making it cheaper to explore outside the current design space so new ideas can run efficiently and more approaches get a chance.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we have to be careful about what we mean by convergence. If many people are using similar architectures, does that mean we have discovered the best architecture, or does it mean those architectures run well on the hardware and software systems we have today? Those are difficult to separate.

The hardware lottery is a useful way to think about that feedback loop. An idea that maps well to existing hardware is easier to scale, so it gets more experimentation and investment. We improve the software around it, which makes it even more attractive. An alternative idea might look less promising simply because it does not have that support yet.

That does not mean the progress is artificial. These models work very well. But I would hesitate to interpret their convergence as evidence that this is the only way forward. From a systems perspective, the interesting question is how we make it cheaper to explore alternatives—through better programming tools, compilers, and hardware—so that our ability to test an idea is less dependent on whether it fits today's dominant computational pattern.

r001.rationale: The response says ideas that map well to current hardware are easier to scale and attract investment, which contributes to the apparent convergence.

r002.rationale: It questions whether convergence shows the architectures are best and says it is not evidence they are the only way forward; alternatives may seem less promising because they lack support.

r003.rationale: The response does not attribute historical breakthroughs to diversity among model approaches.

r004.rationale: It advocates making alternative ideas cheaper to explore through programming tools, compilers, and hardware.
